processing: Fresh leaf goes through three rounds of pan-firing and rolling, then is rubbed into clusters to bring up the down and dried slowly over a gentle heat.
harvest_season: Spring, with a standard of one bud and one leaf recorded under the Xueya name.
appearance_dry: Tender green hooks like tiny fish hooks with soft white down on the back; the Xueya style is described as spiral-curled and very downy.
appearance_wet: Not closely described; young bud and leaf are what the picking standard implies.
taste_profile: Fragrant and full, with a fresh, brisk flavour and a sweet return that holds for about four steeps.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a downy curled green. A little haze from the down is normal. The tea's old reputation is for lasting through four bowls, so do not stop after the first.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring green, and best drunk within the year as usual for this class. Under the Xueya name it has been graded as special, first and second grade. Yunwu and Xueya on a label can refer to the same tea, though the two descriptions differ in shape, so ask or look at the leaf.
description:
Guiding Yunwu comes from Yunwu mountain in Guiding county, south of Guiyang, one of the main peaks of the Miao Ridge. It goes by a pile of names: Niaowang for its earliest growing area at Niaowang pass, Yugou for its fish-hook shape, and Guiding Xueya after 1949. The local Miao name is recorded as bulaoji.

The tea is credited to the Yangwang local variety and a hands-on process of three pan-firings and rollings, a rubbing that lifts the down, and slow drying. The result is small green hooks with a soft white back. Descriptions under the Xueya name speak instead of spirals, which is worth knowing when you compare packets.

In the cup it is fragrant and full with a sweet return, and its reputation rests on lasting through repeat steeps. Moderately hot water suits it.

The protected name covers townships across the county, so Yunwu on the label says less than it seems. Ask for the harvest date and look for even, well-shaped leaf with plenty of down.
history:
Local accounts say the tea was sent as tribute under the Yuan, Ming and Qing and describe a stele recording this, the only one of its kind in Guizhou by the same accounts. The Republican-era Guiding gazetteer is more modest and more quotable: it ranks Guiding Yunwu as the province's most famous tea, says it was hard to obtain for its small output, and calls it a former tribute.

After 1949 it was renamed Guiding Xueya, and the older name has since returned as a geographical indication and certification mark.
